lesson.title: Endpoint Consideration: When the Winning Answer Sits at the Boundary
lesson.summary: An interior critical point is not automatically the answer. Solve a two-shape wire problem where the interior critical point turns out to be a minimum, forcing the true maximum to be found at a domain endpoint instead.
lesson.body:
On a closed interval, the global maximum or minimum of a function can occur either at a critical point or at one of the interval's endpoints, and there is no way to know which without checking both. This is the core warning behind endpoint consideration: finding and verifying an interior critical point tells you it is a local extremum, but it does not automatically tell you it beats every point on the boundary.

Here is a classic scenario where this actually happens. A wire 20 centimeters long is cut into two pieces. One piece is bent into a square, and the other is bent into a circle. Let x be the length of wire used for the square, so 20 - x is the length used for the circle, with practical domain 0 <= x <= 20 (the endpoints are included here because using zero wire for one shape, all of it for the other, is a perfectly valid physical choice).

The square has perimeter x, so each side is x/4, and its area is (x/4)^2 = x^2/16. The circle has circumference 20 - x, so its radius is (20 - x)/(2 pi), and its area is pi times that radius squared, which simplifies to (20 - x)^2/(4 pi). The total enclosed area is A(x) = x^2/16 + (20 - x)^2/(4 pi).

Differentiate: A'(x) = x/8 - (20 - x)/(2 pi). Setting this to zero: x/8 = (20 - x)/(2 pi), which cross multiplies to 2 pi x = 8(20 - x), giving 2 pi x + 8x = 160, so x(2 pi + 8) = 160, and x = 160/(2 pi + 8) = 80/(4 + pi), approximately 11.20 centimeters.

Now check the second derivative before assuming this is the maximum being sought: A''(x) = 1/8 + 1/(2 pi). Both terms are positive no matter what x is, so A''(x) > 0 everywhere, which means this critical point is a minimum of total area, not a maximum. If the goal is to maximize the combined area, the interior critical point is exactly the wrong kind of point to land on, and the true maximum has to be sitting at one of the two endpoints instead.

Evaluate both endpoints directly. At x = 0 (no wire used for the square, all of it becomes a circle): A(0) = 0 + 400/(4 pi) = 100/pi, approximately 31.83 square centimeters. At x = 20 (all wire becomes a square, none left for a circle): A(20) = 400/16 + 0 = 25 square centimeters. Since 100/pi is larger than 25, the maximum total area is achieved at x = 0, meaning the best strategy is not to cut the wire at all, bend the entire length into a circle. For completeness, the interior critical value is A(80/(4+pi)) is approximately 14.0 square centimeters, smaller than both endpoint values, exactly as expected for a minimum sitting between two larger boundary values.

The general habit to take away is this: always evaluate the objective function at the domain's endpoints, even when a verified interior critical point already exists, because the second derivative test can reveal that the critical point is the wrong type for what you were trying to find, a minimum when a maximum was wanted, or vice versa, and in that situation the actual answer to your question is guaranteed to live at a boundary.
